passage:
Dear Chetan,

I'm writing this instead of saying it in the group because I didn't want you to feel singled out.

When we split the survey project, I gave you the data tables since you're quicker with spreadsheets than any of us. It's been ten days and the sheet is still mostly blank. I'm not angry. I'm a bit worried, because the others are waiting on those numbers for their sections.

Is something getting in the way? Too much work from other subjects, something at home, or was the task unclear? If it's the last one, that's on me.

Can we meet Thursday after class for twenty minutes? We can break it into smaller parts, or I can move some to Ruchi.

Either way, you're still on this team.

Vinita

qa.q: When did Vinita suggest meeting Chetan?
qa.a: Vinita suggested Thursday after class, for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What is Vinita worried about, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Vinita is worried the rest of the team is stuck waiting for the numbers; the letter says so directly and still says Vinita is not angry.

qa.q: Which parts of Vinita's letter make it kind but still firm?
qa.a: Vinita asks what is getting in the way, owns a possible share of the problem, and offers concrete options instead of blaming Chetan.

qa.q: If you were Chetan, how might this letter feel?
qa.a: It could feel embarrassing but also relieving, because it gives a private way to explain and a clear chance to fix it. 🙏

grounding: Shows a student leader who divided work handling a teammate's lag with kindness and a concrete plan.

passage: So, yeah, I'm Naveen, and I was the fest coordinator last year, and I thought leading meant doing everything myself. First week, I made one big list and told eight people to pick things. Chaos. Three people picked posters, nobody picked sponsors. After that I sat down and gave each person one clear job and a date. That part worked. The hard part was Jahnavi. She'd promised the stage plan and kept saying 'almost done'. I was annoyed, honestly. But instead of complaining in the group, I asked her for chai. Turned out her mother was in hospital and she was too embarrassed to say. We paired her with someone, and she still did the lighting beautifully. I learned the direction has to be clear, but people aren't machines.

qa.q: How many people did Naveen first ask to pick tasks from a list?
qa.a: Naveen asked eight people.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi likely feeling when she kept saying 'almost done'?
qa.a: She was probably stressed and embarrassed, because her mother was in hospital and she did not want to admit she was falling behind.

qa.q: Which of Naveen's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Giving each person one clear job and date removed confusion, and talking privately to Jahnavi uncovered the real problem.

qa.q: What would have changed if Naveen had complained about Jahnavi in the group?
qa.a: She might have felt shamed and hidden her situation even more, and the stage work could have stayed stuck.

grounding: Shows a young leader learning to set clear roles and to handle a struggling teammate privately and kindly.

passage: I'm Uday, and I was in Wasim's group for the robotics project. I'll tell you what I saw. On day one he drew the whole robot on the whiteboard and wrote our names next to parts: me on wiring, Soham on code, Parth on the frame. Nobody argued, because it was clear. Around week three Parth kept missing lab sessions. Some of us wanted to report him. Wasim didn't. He waited after class, walked Parth to the canteen, and they talked for a while. I don't know what was said. Next day Parth came with half the frame done and Wasim had quietly taken one small part off his list. Parth never missed again. Wasim looked tired that week, but he never once raised his voice.

qa.q: Which part of the robot did Uday work on?
qa.a: Uday was put on the wiring.

qa.q: What might Wasim have been thinking when he chose not to report Parth?
qa.a: He was probably concerned about why Parth kept missing sessions and wanted to understand before treating it as a discipline problem.

qa.q: What could other student leaders learn from how Wasim divided the work?
qa.a: Drawing the whole project and naming who owns each part makes roles clear from the start and avoids arguments.

qa.q: How might Parth have seen Wasim's approach?
qa.a: He likely felt given a fair chance instead of being exposed, which may be why he started showing up again.

grounding: Shows an observer describing a peer leader setting direction and handling underperformance quietly and kindly.

passage: Day 1: Farhan, chosen to lead the four-person robotics project, opened the meeting with, 'Goal: a working prototype in three weeks.' He wrote the tasks on the board and let each person pick one. Naveen chose the sensor wiring. Day 9: The wiring still wasn't done, and the others were grumbling in the group chat. Farhan was tempted to post something sharp. Instead he found Naveen in the canteen. 'The sensors are stuck. What's going on?' Naveen admitted he had never soldered before and was too embarrassed to say so. Farhan paired him with Riya for two evenings and moved the deadline for that part by three days, telling the team why. Day 19: The prototype rolled across the lab floor. Naveen demonstrated the sensor part to the professor, a little proudly.

qa.q: Which task did Naveen choose?
qa.a: The sensor wiring.

qa.q: Why hadn't Naveen told anyone about the wiring problem?
qa.a: He had never soldered before and felt too embarrassed to admit it.

qa.q: What did Farhan try instead of posting something sharp, and why did it work?
qa.a: He spoke to Naveen privately, found the real reason, paired him with Riya and openly adjusted the deadline, fixing the problem without shaming him.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team have seen Farhan's decision?
qa.a: They had been grumbling, but his explanation of the new deadline helped them understand it and trust how he handled things.

grounding: Shows a student leader setting a goal, dividing tasks and handling a teammate's underperformance kindly over three weeks.

passage: Ankita, you look exactly how I looked at twenty-one, when they made me supervisor of the packing line at the biscuit factory in Aurangabad. Four women, all older than me. For a month I did half their work myself because I was scared to tell them what to do. I went home aching, and they thought I didn't trust them. One of them, Rukmini, finally said, 'Jyoti madam, tell us the target and let us plan.' Oof. So I did. Every morning I said the day's number and asked who would take which part. When one lady kept falling behind, I asked her quietly, away from the others, and learned she couldn't read the small labels well. We moved her to cartons. See, leading isn't doing it all. It's giving direction and noticing people.

qa.q: What was Jyoti put in charge of at twenty-one?
qa.a: The packing line at the biscuit factory, supervising four women older than her.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti do half the work herself at first?
qa.a: She was scared to tell older women what to do.

qa.q: How did Jyoti handle the worker who kept falling behind?
qa.a: She asked her quietly, away from the others, learned she could not read the small labels well, and moved her to cartons.

qa.q: How did the women on the line see Jyoti doing their work?
qa.a: They thought she did not trust them, which is why Rukmini asked her simply to give the target.

grounding: A senior woman recalls learning to lead a small team by giving direction and handling a struggling worker kindly.

passage: Three days before the final-year project demo, Hemant's team was a mess. The app ran, but the report was half-written and Raghav's database section was still empty. The others were already muttering about "freeloaders". Then the hostel lost power for a whole evening. Hemant called a meeting by phone torchlight. "Before anything: Raghav, can we talk after?" Outside on the steps, Raghav admitted he had been doing night shifts at a courier depot since his father's hours were cut. "I didn't want to say." Hemant took a breath. "Okay. Can you do the part only you can, explaining the tables, and I'll take the formatting?" Raghav nodded. Back inside, Hemant split what was left into three lists with names and times, and put his own name on the worst job. Raghav's section arrived at 6 a.m., short and correct.

qa.q: Where had Raghav been doing night shifts?
qa.a: At a courier depot.

qa.q: What might Hemant have been feeling as he called the meeting by torchlight?
qa.a: Hemant was probably stressed about the deadline and uneasy about the muttering, but determined to understand before blaming.

qa.q: How did Hemant handle underperformance kindly and still meet the deadline?
qa.a: He talked to Raghav privately, fitted the work to Raghav's situation, gave everyone clear names and times, and took the worst job himself.

qa.q: How might Raghav have experienced being spoken to privately?
qa.a: Raghav probably felt relieved and respected, able to explain the night shifts without being shamed in front of everyone.

grounding: Under a deadline and a power cut, a student team lead divides work clearly and handles a struggling member kindly.

passage: Elizabeth had four weekends to run the Saturday food drive for her church youth group in Chennai, and a team of five. At the first meeting she wrote one sentence on the whiteboard: "Two hundred ration kits to the families on the Adyar list by the 28th." Then she gave each person one job: donors, packing, transport, list-checking; she took whatever fell through. By week two, Gopika, on donor calls, had made only three. Elizabeth felt annoyed, then remembered Gopika had just started a new job. Over filter coffee she asked, "Is the calling hard, or is the time hard?" "The calling," Gopika admitted. "I hate asking for things." They swapped: Gopika took the packing lists, which she was brilliant at, and Elizabeth made ten donor calls herself and paired the rest with a bolder volunteer. On the 28th they delivered one hundred and eighty-six kits.

qa.q: How many ration kits did they deliver on the 28th?
qa.a: One hundred and eighty-six kits.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she saw Gopika had made only three calls?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt annoyed at first, then more understanding once she remembered Gopika's new job.

qa.q: Why was Elizabeth's question over coffee a good way to handle the problem?
qa.a: It asked about the cause without blame, which revealed a task mismatch rather than laziness and led to a better swap.

qa.q: What was it like for Gopika to admit she hates asking for things?
qa.a: Gopika probably felt embarrassed but relieved to say it, and then capable once she had a job that suited her.

grounding: A young volunteer leader sets a clear goal, divides work, and kindly re-matches a struggling teammate.

passage:
"Hafsa, got a minute before the evening rush?" Dolma asked, wiping her hands.
Hafsa froze by the milk steamer. "Did I mess up an order again?"
"Two today. I'm not angry. I want to understand."
"The tickets come so fast, I panic and skip one."
"Okay. What would help?"
"I don't know. Maybe if I wasn't on the machine and the till at once?"
Dolma nodded. "That's on me. I gave you two stations in your second week. From tonight, machine only. Tenzin takes the till."
"Won't he mind?"
"He's done both for a year. He'll survive." Dolma smiled. "And line up the tickets left to right, oldest first. Read each one out as you start it."
"Out loud? People will hear."
"That's the idea. If you call it, we all know."
Hafsa breathed out. "Okay. Machine only. Out loud."
"And Hafsa? Your cappuccinos are already better than mine."

qa.q: Which station will Hafsa do from tonight?
qa.a: The machine only.

qa.q: What was Hafsa worried about when Dolma called her over?
qa.a: Hafsa was anxious she had messed up an order again and expected to be scolded.

qa.q: How did Dolma handle the mistakes kindly but clearly?
qa.a: She named the two errors without anger, asked what would help, took responsibility for giving two stations too soon, and set a clear new routine.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel about taking the till?
qa.a: Tenzin, experienced at both, will probably manage easily, maybe with mild grumbling, and may appreciate the clearer division.

grounding: A young café shift lead addresses a new worker's mistakes kindly, restructures the work and gives a clear method.

passage:
When I became team lead at twenty-two, I thought leading meant doing the hardest parts myself. I set big goals, then worked till midnight fixing everyone's work.
One teammate, Arnab, kept missing deadlines. I was frustrated. My first thought was to complain to my manager.
Instead, I asked him for chai. I said, "I've noticed deadlines slipping. What's going on?"
He admitted he didn't understand the new software and was too embarrassed to ask. His father had also been unwell.
We split his tasks into smaller pieces, and I paired him with a teammate for a week. He caught up.
I'm Ramesh. I learnt leading isn't doing everything. It's making sure everyone can do their part.

qa.q: What did Arnab not understand?
qa.a: The new software.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling about Arnab's missed deadlines at first?
qa.a: Ramesh felt frustrated and was tempted to complain to the manager.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do that handled underperformance kindly?
qa.a: Ramesh talked privately, asked what was going on, broke tasks into smaller pieces and paired Arnab with a teammate.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt when Ramesh asked him for chai?
qa.a: Arnab probably felt nervous at first, then relieved to explain.

grounding: A young team lead recalls handling a teammate's underperformance with understanding.

passage:
Project supervisor's note.
Harish is leading a five-person student team for the city waste survey. At the start, he gave vague instructions and the team worked on overlapping parts.
This week he changed. He wrote a clear goal on the board, split the survey into areas, and gave each person one area with a deadline.
Lavanya, one of the members, had submitted nothing for two weeks. Harish didn't shout. I watched him ask her quietly after the meeting. She said she was overwhelmed with part-time work. He gave her a smaller area and a later deadline, and checked in on Wednesday.
The team finished on time. — Dr. Kapoor

qa.q: How many people are on Harish's team?
qa.a: Five people.

qa.q: What was Lavanya likely feeling when she had submitted nothing?
qa.a: Lavanya was probably overwhelmed and stressed by her part-time work.

qa.q: What did Harish do that improved the team?
qa.a: He gave a clear goal, split the work into areas with deadlines, and handled Lavanya's struggle privately and kindly.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team see Harish's change?
qa.a: They likely feel less confused and more confident in him as a leader.

grounding: A supervisor notes a young leader setting direction and handling underperformance kindly.

passage:
Dear Diary,
First week as team lead for the app project. Five people. I felt proud and terrified.
Wasim hasn't finished anything. Today in the meeting, I almost snapped at him in front of everyone. I stopped myself.
After, I messaged him: "Can we talk for ten minutes?" He was defensive at first. Then he said he'd been given the hardest module and didn't know where to start.
That's on me. I divided the work without asking anyone what they were good at.
So tomorrow: I'll ask everyone their strengths and reassign. I'll pair Wasim with Priyam on the module. And I'll say sorry for not asking earlier.
— Jahnavi

qa.q: How many people are on Jahnavi's team?
qa.a: Five people.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling in the meeting when almost snapping?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt frustrated and stressed about Wasim's lack of progress.

qa.q: What will Jahnavi do differently tomorrow?
qa.a: Ask everyone their strengths, reassign work, pair Wasim with Priyam and apologise for not asking earlier.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel after the private talk?
qa.a: Wasim likely feels relieved and less alone with the hard module.

grounding: In a diary a young team lead handles underperformance kindly and adjusts how work is divided.

passage:
Lokesh was twenty and leading a group of eight college volunteers at a flood relief camp in a small town in Assam. He set the plan each morning: two sorting supplies, three cooking, three with the local health team.
Irawati kept disappearing from the cooking shift. By day three, the others were grumbling. "Why do we cover for her?"
Lokesh found her sitting behind the school building, pale. "Irawati, what's going on?"
She admitted the smoke from the cooking fires gave her headaches and made her eyes stream, and she was embarrassed to say so when others were working so hard.
"You could've told me. Let's switch you to sorting supplies. Can you also keep the list of what we're short of?"
She did it brilliantly. At the evening meeting, Lokesh said only, "We've changed roles to fit people better," and the grumbling stopped.

qa.q: How many volunteers was Lokesh leading?
qa.a: A group of eight college volunteers.

qa.q: How was Irawati feeling when Lokesh found her?
qa.a: Irawati felt unwell and embarrassed, not wanting to complain while others worked hard.

qa.q: Which of Lokesh's choices showed good team leadership?
qa.a: He asked privately before blaming, moved Irawati to work that suited her, and explained the change to the team without exposing her.

qa.q: How might the grumbling volunteers see Lokesh's explanation?
qa.a: They might feel reassured that the workload was being handled fairly, even without knowing Irawati's reason.

grounding: Shows a young leader dividing work and handling a volunteer's underperformance kindly.

passage:
Pablo was leading a four-person student startup team in Barcelona, building an app for local markets. He set weekly goals every Monday and split the tasks. Selin, the designer, had missed two deadlines in a row.
The others wanted to drop her. Pablo invited her for coffee instead. "The last two weeks have been hard for us. What's going on for you?"
Selin was quiet, then said she didn't understand what "done" meant for her tasks. The briefs were vague, and she'd been too proud to ask.
Pablo felt a pang; the briefs were his. "That's on me too. Let's write clear ones together, with examples."
They did. He also set a Wednesday check-in, fifteen minutes, just the two of them.
Selin delivered the next design two days early. At the Monday meeting, Pablo said, "Clearer briefs helped all of us," and moved on.

qa.q: What did Selin say she didn't understand?
qa.a: What "done" meant for her tasks, because the briefs were vague.

qa.q: What does Pablo feeling a pang suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Pablo felt guilty, realising his vague briefs were part of the problem.

qa.q: What could other student leaders learn from Pablo's approach?
qa.a: Talk privately before judging, check whether your own instructions are clear, and add short check-ins.

qa.q: How might Selin have felt when Pablo said it was on him too?
qa.a: Selin probably felt relieved and respected, less alone with the blame.

grounding: Illustrates a young team leader setting direction and handling underperformance kindly, including owning his part.

passage: The college magazine office smelled of old paper and marker ink. Sonali, the new student editor, had split the issue three ways: features to her, photos to Aman, interviews to Sudha. Two deadlines had passed without Sudha's interviews, and the others were muttering. Sonali could have posted about it in the group chat. Instead she found Sudha alone after the Thursday meeting. "The interviews are late, and I need them by Monday for the printer. What's getting in the way?" Sudha's eyes went to the floor. "My mother's been in and out of hospital. I didn't want to use it as an excuse." Sonali let that sit for a moment. "Thanks for telling me. Can you do two interviews instead of four? I'll take the other two." Sudha breathed out. "Two I can do." That evening Sonali updated the plan without mentioning why.

qa.q: By when did Sonali need the interviews?
qa.a: She needed them by Monday for the printer.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when Sonali asked what was getting in the way?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and anxious, looking at the floor and worried that her mother's illness would sound like an excuse.

qa.q: What did Sonali's approach get right as a team lead?
qa.a: She raised the problem privately, stated the deadline clearly, asked what was blocking, and cut the load instead of blaming Sudha in public 👍

qa.q: How might the muttering teammates see the updated plan?
qa.a: They may just see the work moving again without knowing Sudha's private reason, which protects her dignity.

grounding: Shows a young team leader setting direction, dividing work and handling a teammate's underperformance kindly.
